newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank denies row with Waigel, lodges protest.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank denies row with Waigel, lodges protest.

text.p: The Bundesbank has sent a letter to Germany's respected weekly newspaper Die Zeit complaining about an article carried in this week's edition, Bundesbank spokesman Manfred Koerber said on Friday.

Die Zeit this week reported that there was a rift between Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer and Finance Minister Theo Waigel over a planned European "stability pact" to ensure fiscal discipline within European monetary union.
Koerber, who was quoted in the article alongside Tietmeyer, Waigel and other officials, said in answer to Reuter enquiries that his letter, made clear that the report was not accurate.
The letter was sent to the newspaper in his official capacity as Bundesbank spokesman.

"The Bundesbank and its president unreservedly support the efforts of the federal finance minister to ensure that the participants in a common currency pursue stability-oriented fiscal policies with the aid of a stability pact," Koerber quoted the letter as saying.

He said he also pointed out that Tietmeyer himself had made this clear in Dublin on September 21 at the end of an informal summit meeting of European Union central bank governors and finance ministers.

The Dublin meeting sketched out the broad outline of a stability pact which would impose sanctions for countries which overspent, taking their budget deficit to more than three percent of gross domestic product.
But many of the details of the pact -- including the size of the fines and exactly how they will be enforced -- were left unresolved at that meeting.
Tietmeyer told reporters at the end of the talks that there had been good progress madde, adding "You cannot expect to decide everything in one meeting."
German officials -- at both the Bundesbank and the Finance Ministry -- have made clear they want the final pact, which was originally proposed by Waigel, to be as stringent as possible.
However they are expected to face calls from other European Union members to make compromises on some of their demands.
